passages.t: ‘Many a time they have persecuted me from my youth’
passages.happening:
Psalm 129 is another call and response. “A song of ascents. Many a time they have persecuted me from my youth” (verse 1). The leader tells the people to say it with him, and they repeat it, adding, “but they have not prevailed against me” (verse 2).

Then a cruel picture. “The plowmen plowed over my back; they made their furrows long” (verse 3). But it did not last. “The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the cords of the wicked” (verse 4).

The second half is a prayer against those who hate Zion. “May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame” (verse 5). “May they be like grass on the rooftops, which withers before it can grow” (verse 6). It gives no harvest for anyone to gather (verse 7). And no one passing by will greet them with a blessing in the LORD's name (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
‘My youth’ means Israel's beginnings. The prophets spoke that way of the years in Egypt and the desert: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son” (Hosea 11:1). Since then the nation had been attacked again and again. Psalm 129 looks back over all of it, as Psalm 124 did, and says: they hurt us, but they did not finish us. The note on Psalm 120 explains the Songs of Ascents.

A plough was pulled by oxen and cut long furrows through the ground. To have ploughmen plough your back is a picture of deep wounds, perhaps from whipping, or of a people forced to lie down while others walk over them. Isaiah used that second picture (Isaiah 51:23). ‘The cords’ in verse 4 may be the ropes that tied the plough to the oxen. God cut them, and the ploughing stopped.

Houses had flat roofs of packed earth. Seeds blew onto them and sprouted after rain, but with no depth of soil they withered in the sun. No one could harvest them. At harvest, people greeted the workers with a blessing. In Ruth, Boaz greets his harvesters with “The LORD be with you” (Ruth 2:4), and they answer, “The LORD bless you” (Ruth 2:4). Grass on the roof never gets that greeting.
passages.later:
Jesus told of seed that fell on rocky ground: “they withered because they had no root” (Matthew 13:6).

Paul described the life of the apostles in words close to verse 2: “persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed” (2 Corinthians 4:9).
passages.hard: Verses 5 to 8 pray that those who hate Zion come to nothing. This is a mild example of the cursing psalms. It asks that their hatred fail, not that blood be shed. The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out how Christians read such prayers. No reading of it makes it right to harm anyone, and it names no people of today.
passages.asks:
‘They have not prevailed against me.’ Many people carry long scars: years of being mistreated, or a family history of pain. Psalm 129 does not pretend the wounds were small. It says the furrows were long. But it also says the cords were cut.

Can you look back over your own story and see where God brought an end to something that might have destroyed you? Say it, as Israel did, out loud.
